findings.title: Device limit only enforced on first request; cache entry lets rejected devices in afterwards
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` writes the device key to the local cache before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, and it does not remove the key when that call fails. When the limit is hit, the first request returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and `Authenticate` rejects it. Every later request from the same device in the next ~29 minutes hits the cache and returns nil, so `Authenticate` succeeds. The limit therefore only rejects a device's first request and is not actually enforced. Fix by evicting the key on error, or by setting the cache only after a successful store call.

findings.title: Count-then-insert is not atomic; limit can be exceeded under concurrency
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then does a separate INSERT, with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first requests from new devices, or several Grafana instances sharing one DB, can all read `count < limit` and all insert. The configured limit can then be exceeded by an arbitrary amount.

findings.title: rowsAffected==0 treated as limit reached; false positives on MySQL
findings.body: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. By default MySQL reports only rows whose values actually changed, not rows matched. `updated_at` has second precision, so an existing, already-counted device re-tagged within the same second with the same IP and user agent changes nothing and gets 0 rows. That device is then wrongly rejected as over the limit.

findings.title: Device limit bypassed by omitting the device ID header
findings.body: `TagDevice` returns nil when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing, and it also returns nil when the IP cannot be parsed. In both cases anonymous authentication succeeds without any limit check. Any client can get unlimited anonymous access by not sending the header, so the limit is advisory at best.

findings.title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path
findings.body: Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and panic recovery. It now runs inline in `Authenticate`, using the request context. When a limit is configured, each new device costs an extra COUNT(*) query plus a write. Slow-DB latency, or a panic in this path, now directly affects every anonymous request. The previous panic protection was also removed.

findings.title: Provider signature changes likely break wire DI
findings.body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` now takes `db.DB` instead of `anonstore.AnonStore`. `ProvideAnonDBStore` now takes an extra `int64` that wire cannot supply. No wire set (wire.go / wireexts) is updated in this PR. If `ProvideAnonDBStore` is still registered as a provider there, wire generation fails. Otherwise the unused binding should be removed.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit inferred as type `undefined`
findings.body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the class property type as `undefined`, not `number | undefined`. Consumers of `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` cannot use it as a number without casting. Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

findings.title: No test that existing devices can still be updated at the limit
findings.body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a new device is rejected once the limit is reached. No test checks that an already-registered device is still updated successfully at the limit, which is the `updateDevice` path. No test covers the authn client behaviour either, including repeat requests after a rejection.
